skills.name: Prepare ammonia and describe its properties

note.text:
Laboratory preparation: heat an ammonium salt with an alkali.
2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 → CaCl2 + 2NH3 + 2H2O
The gas is dried with quicklime (not concentrated sulphuric acid, which would react with it) and collected by upward delivery, because it is less dense than air and extremely soluble in water.
Physical properties: a colourless gas with a sharp, pungent smell; less dense than air (relative molecular mass 17); extremely soluble in water, as the fountain experiment shows; easily liquefied.
Chemical properties:
• Alkaline: its solution turns damp red litmus blue, the only common alkaline gas.
• With acids it gives ammonium salts: NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl, seen as dense white fumes.
• A reducing agent: it reduces heated copper(II) oxide, 3CuO + 2NH3 → 3Cu + N2 + 3H2O.
• It burns in oxygen, but not in air.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to prepare ammonia, explain how it is dried and collected, and describe it as an alkaline gas and a reducing agent.
Builds on: Lesson {11} (nitrogen) and Form Three acids, bases and salts.
Leads to: Lesson {17} (fertilisers made from ammonia) and the Haber process.

sections.heading: Preparation and collection
sections.text:
Heat an ammonium salt with an alkali:
{2}{formula('NH4Cl')} + {formula('Ca(OH)2')} → {formula('CaCl2')} + {2}{formula('NH3')} + {2}{formula('H2O')}
The mixture is heated in a slanting tube, so that the water that condenses runs away from the hot glass.
Drying: with QUICKLIME, {formula('CaO')}. Concentrated sulphuric acid cannot be used, because the acid would react with the alkaline gas; anhydrous calcium chloride also forms a compound with it.
Collection: by upward delivery into an inverted jar, because ammonia is less dense than air (relative molecular mass {17}) and far too soluble to collect over water.

sections.heading: Properties
sections.text:
Ammonia is a colourless gas with a sharp, pungent smell. It is extremely soluble in water: in the fountain experiment, a few drops of water in a flask of the gas lower the pressure so much that water rushes in as a fountain.
• ALKALINE: it is the only common alkaline gas, and turns damp red litmus blue.
• With acids it gives ammonium salts: {formula('NH3')} + {formula('HCl')} → {formula('NH4Cl')}, seen as dense white fumes. This is the test for the gas.
• REDUCING agent: {3}{formula('CuO')} + {2}{formula('NH3')} → {3}Cu + {formula('N2')} + {3}{formula('H2O')}. The black solid turns pink-brown.
• It burns in pure oxygen but not in air.

key_words.meaning: a gas whose solution is an alkali; ammonia is the only common one
calcium oxide, {formula('CaO')}, a basic drying agent
collecting a gas less dense than air in an inverted jar
a demonstration of how soluble ammonia is

mistake.wrong: ammonia is dried with concentrated sulphuric acid
mistake.why: The acid reacts with the alkaline gas to give ammonium sulphate, so the gas would be lost.

worked_example.problem: Explain why ammonia is dried with quicklime and not with concentrated sulphuric acid.
steps: A drying agent must remove water without reacting with the gas.
Concentrated sulphuric acid is an acid, so it would react with the ammonia to give ammonium sulphate.
Quicklime, {formula('CaO')}, is a basic oxide, so it dries the gas without reacting with it.
worked_example.answer: because sulphuric acid would react with the alkaline gas, while quicklime does not

cards.idea: An ammonium salt heated with an alkali gives ammonia.
Ammonia is the only common alkaline gas: it turns damp red litmus blue.
example: with {formula('HCl')} it gives dense white fumes of {formula('NH4Cl')}

cards.idea: Ammonia is a reducing agent: it reduces heated copper(II) oxide to copper.

pick.q: Ammonia is passed over heated copper(II) oxide. Which statement is correct?
pick.r: The copper(II) oxide is reduced to copper, and the ammonia is oxidised to nitrogen
w: The copper(II) oxide is oxidised and the ammonia reduced
e: Losing oxygen is reduction, so it is the copper(II) oxide that is reduced.
The colour change from black to pink-brown shows a clear reaction.
In any redox reaction one substance is oxidised while the other is reduced.

pick.q: What colour change is seen when ammonia reduces heated copper(II) oxide?
e: That is what happens when copper is heated in air: the opposite change.
No white solid is formed; copper metal is pink-brown.
Blue to white is what happens to copper(II) sulphate crystals when they are dehydrated.
pick.y: The black copper(II) oxide becomes pink-brown copper as the oxygen is taken away.

pick.q: Which gas is formed from the ammonia when it reduces copper(II) oxide?
e: The hydrogen of the ammonia ends up in the water that is formed.
The oxygen comes FROM the copper oxide and also ends up in the water.
Nitrogen dioxide needs more oxygen; the product here is nitrogen itself.
pick.y: The nitrogen of the ammonia is set free as {formula('N2')}, and its hydrogen becomes water.

pick.q: Why does ammonia burn in pure oxygen but not in air?
pick.r: Air holds too little oxygen to keep the flame going
w: Ammonia is not flammable at all
The nitrogen in air puts the flame out by reacting
e: It does burn, as the experiment in pure oxygen shows.
Nitrogen does not react; it simply dilutes the oxygen.
Temperature is not the difference; the proportion of oxygen is.
pick.y: In pure oxygen ammonia burns with a greenish-yellow flame; in air, with only {21} per cent oxygen, it will not.

pick.q: Which reagents are used to prepare ammonia in the laboratory?
pick.r: An ammonium salt and an alkali, heated: ammonium chloride with calcium hydroxide
w: Ammonium chloride and dilute hydrochloric acid
A nitrate and a dilute acid
e: An acid would give no ammonia; an ALKALI drives it out of an ammonium salt.
Nitrogen and water do not react; the Haber process uses hydrogen, not water.
A nitrate with a dilute acid gives no ammonia.

pick.r: By upward delivery, because it is less dense than air
e: Its relative molecular mass is {17}, well below the average for air, so it rises.
It is extremely soluble in water, so none would be collected.
There is no need for mercury; an inverted jar works.
pick.y: A gas less dense than air and very soluble is collected by upward delivery into an inverted jar.

pick.q: Which drying agent is used for ammonia?
e: Concentrated sulphuric acid is acidic and reacts with ammonia to give ammonium sulphate.
Phosphorus(V) oxide is acidic and also reacts with ammonia.
Anhydrous calcium chloride forms a compound with ammonia, so it cannot be used.
pick.y: An alkaline gas must be dried with a basic drying agent, and quicklime is the usual choice.

pick.q: What is seen in the fountain experiment with ammonia?
pick.r: Water rushes up into the flask as a fountain, turning red if litmus is present
w: The water stays where it is
The gas bubbles out through the water
e: The gas dissolves so fast that the pressure in the flask falls at once.
No crack is needed; the pressure difference drives the fountain.
The gas is taken INTO the water, not pushed out.
pick.y: Ammonia is extremely soluble, so a drop of water lowers the pressure in the flask and the rest is pushed in.

pick.q: Ammonia gas meets hydrogen chloride gas. What is seen?
pick.r: Dense white fumes of ammonium chloride
e: A brown gas is nitrogen dioxide, which is not formed here.
The solid formed is white, not yellow.
The white fumes are easy to see and are used as a test.
pick.y: {formula('NH3')} + {formula('HCl')} → {formula('NH4Cl')}: the two gases meet and form a white smoke of fine solid.

pick.q: Ammonia is passed over heated copper(II) oxide. What is seen, and what does it show?
pick.r: The black solid turns pink-brown; ammonia is acting as a reducing agent
w: The black solid turns white; ammonia is acting as an acid
The solid is unchanged; ammonia is unreactive
A yellow solid forms; ammonia is acting as an oxidising agent
e: No white solid is formed, and ammonia is alkaline, not acidic.
The reaction is clear, and the copper(II) oxide is reduced to copper.
The ammonia is oxidised here, so it is the reducing agent.
pick.y: {3}{formula('CuO')} + {2}{formula('NH3')} → {3}Cu + {formula('N2')} + {3}{formula('H2O')}: the copper oxide is reduced to copper.

pick.r: Damp red litmus paper turns blue
pick.w1: Damp blue litmus paper turns red
pick.y: Ammonia is the only common alkaline gas, so it turns RED litmus blue.

pick.r: A rod dipped in concentrated hydrochloric acid gives dense white fumes
pick.w1: A rod dipped in acid gives a brown gas
pick.w2: A lighted splint burns more brightly
pick.w3: The gas turns lead(II) ethanoate paper black
pick.y: {formula('NH3')} + {formula('HCl')} → {formula('NH4Cl')}, a white solid that appears as a smoke.

pick.r: It has a sharp pungent smell and turns damp red litmus blue
pick.w2: It has no smell at all
pick.w3: It smells sweet and turns limewater milky
pick.y: The smell with the litmus test together identify ammonia.

questions.prompt: What mass of ammonia, in grams, is there in {n} mol of the gas?

misconceptions.explain: Use the formula {formula('NH3')}, which includes the {3} hydrogen atoms.

solution: The relative molecular mass of {formula('NH3')} is {molarMass('NH3')}.

questions.prompt: What volume of ammonia, in dm³ at s.t.p., is given off when {n} mol of ammonium chloride is heated with excess calcium hydroxide?

misconceptions.explain: The ratio is {2} to {2}, that is {1} mol of gas for each {1} mol of the salt.
The question asks for a volume in dm³, not a mass in grams.

solution: {2} mol of {formula('NH4Cl')} gives {2} mol of {formula('NH3')}, so {n} mol gives {n} mol.
